it-deep-chianti-rufina.title: Rufina
it-deep-chianti-rufina.atlas_note: Rufina is one of the old Chianti zones, in the Sieve valley north east of Florence at the foot of the Apennines. Its higher part, Pomino, reaches 750 m and has grown French varieties since 1855. The climate has hot summers, cold winters and wide temperature swings. Chianti Rufina is a Sangiovese-based sottozona of Chianti, delimited in 1932.
geology: Hills of the Sieve valley at the foot of the Apennines. The only official soil text found is for Pomino, inside the Rufina area: mainly sandstone and marl soils, siliceous and micaceous, with little clay.
Sandstone and marl soils (Pomino)
Mainly arenaceous and marly, with prevailing siliceous and micaceous content and little clay (Pomino art. 9).
climate: Strong temperature swings, hot summers and harsh winters (Pomino art. 9).
550 to 700 mm depending on the year (art. 9).
Chianti Rufina lies in the Val di Sieve, 20 km north east of Florence.
it-deep-chianti-rufina.altitude_text: Pomino vineyards lie between 300 and 750 m (art. 9); new plantings no higher than 650 m for red and 800 m for white (art. 4.1). No official altitude range was found for Chianti Rufina itself.
history: The bando of 24 September 1716 protected the name 'Pomino', which then covered both the Pomino and Rufina areas. (secondary source)
Vittorio degli Albizi introduced French varieties at Pomino, among them Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Blanc, Chardonnay and Sauvignon (Pomino art. 9).
Rufina was one of the zones delimited by the DM of 31 July 1932.
Pomino DOC by DPR of 25 February 1983.
grapes: Base of Chianti Rufina, a sottozona of the Chianti DOCG (art. 1.1).
study_points: Chianti Rufina is in the Val di Sieve, 20 km north east of Florence; a zoning study found 11 vocational units.
Pomino vineyards: 300 to 750 m; 550 to 700 mm of rain (art. 9).
Pomino was one of the four zones of the 1716 edict. (secondary source)
Rufina is a sottozona of the Chianti DOCG (art. 1.1).

region.vine_area_src: Vineyard area (superficie vitata) of Piemonte for 2024, 44,471 ha, in the official series published by Regione Piemonte and Vignaioli Piemontesi in L'Annata Vitivinicola in Piemonte 2025 (Dec 2025): 2016 43,500; 2017 44,202; 2018 44,449; 2019 44,677; 2020 44,737; 2021 45,420; 2022 45,823 (peak); 2023 44,285; 2024 44,471; 2025 43,792 (estimate, final figure due January 2026). The 2024 figure was first given as provisional in January 2025 and is unchanged in the December 2025 series. Other measures for 2024: 43,670 ha suitable for DO wine and 36,193 ha claimed for DO wine at the 2024 harvest (Regione Piemonte, Qualche dato sul vino piemontese oggi); 39,400 ha in the ISTAT crop statistics; about 46,000 ha in AGEA data for 2025 (I numeri del vino).
region.grape_share_note: Percent of 41,699 ha, the 2024 total of the Regione Piemonte register (Anagrafe Agricola del Piemonte) as extracted and published by David Way (Winefriend, Apr 2025): Barbera 10,099 ha, Moscato Bianco 9,833, Nebbiolo 6,835, Dolcetto 3,115, Cortese 2,680, Arneis 1,346, Chardonnay 1,286, Pinot Nero 735, Timorasso 439, Erbaluce 322. Shares computed by us. The register itself could not be read, so this is a secondary reproduction of official data. A later Way article (2026), from the same register, gives different 2024 areas (Barbera 10,762, Moscato Bianco 10,426, Nebbiolo 7,313, Dolcetto 3,308, Timorasso 478) and preliminary 2026 areas on a total of about 42,000 ha (Barbera 9,897, Moscato Bianco 9,849, Nebbiolo 7,192, Dolcetto 2,867, Timorasso 560, Erbaluce 324), so the two extractions differ. Both put Barbera and Moscato Bianco near 24% each and Nebbiolo near 16 to 17%.
region.atlas_note: Piedmont had 44,471 ha of vines in 2024 by the regional count, mostly on the hills of the provinces of Cuneo, Asti and Alessandria south of the Po, with smaller areas in the north around Novara, Vercelli, Biella and Turin. Barbera and Moscato Bianco are the most planted grapes, followed by Nebbiolo, which has grown fast while Dolcetto has fallen. The region has 19 DOCG and 41 DOC and no IGT, and about 93% of its wine is DO wine. The vineyard area peaked at 45,823 ha in 2022 and is shrinking as growers grub up vines.

Alta Langa.atlas_note: Alta Langa is a traditional method sparkling wine DOCG on the high hills of the Langhe, Roero and Monferrato, in the provinces of Cuneo, Asti and Alessandria. It is made from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay. Only vintage dated wines are allowed. The area under vine has grown fast since the DOCG was granted.
rules: Pinot Nero and/or Chardonnay 90 to 100%; other non-aromatic varieties suited to Piemonte up to 10% (art. 2)

Asti.atlas_note: Asti DOCG covers the Moscato Bianco hills of the provinces of Asti, Cuneo and Alessandria, in 51 communes. It has two main wines: Asti (Asti Spumante), a fully sparkling sweet wine, and Moscato d'Asti, a lightly sparkling wine with low alcohol. It is the largest DOCG in Piedmont by volume. A Metodo Classico and late harvest versions are also allowed.

Barolo.atlas_note: Whole commune in the zone (art. 3). In 2018 the Consorzio counted just over 260 ha of Nebbiolo da Barolo, 41 wineries and 37 MGA. Brunate, Cerequio and Fossati (with La Morra), Bussia (with Monforte d'Alba) and Ravera (with Novello) cross its border.

region.vine_area_src: Planted vineyard area in the ARTEA schedario viticolo at 31 July 2024 (Regione Toscana, presentation of 3 Feb 2025). Of this, 58,079 ha (94.5%) is eligible for DOCG or DOC. ISMEA-based press material gave almost 61,000 ha in Feb 2024.
region.grape_share_note: Shares of the 61,431 ha regional vineyard, computed from the hectares per variety in the Regione Toscana 2025 presentation (ARTEA schedario, 2024). The Feb 2024 PrimAnteprima release gave Sangiovese 59%, Merlot 8%, Cabernet Sauvignon 6%, Trebbiano Toscano 4%, Vermentino 3%.
region.atlas_note: Tuscany had 61,431 ha of vineyard in 2024, held by 12,479 farms. Siena (20,789 ha) and Florence (17,130 ha) hold most of it, then Grosseto, Arezzo and Livorno. Sangiovese covers 57% of the vineyard and is the base of almost every red DOCG. The region has 11 DOCG and 41 DOC, and 94.5% of the vineyard is eligible for a DOP. Chianti and Chianti Classico together make up about 62% of the claimed DOP area.

Brunello di Montalcino.atlas_note: Brunello comes from the single commune of Montalcino in the province of Siena. It is a varietal Sangiovese, locally called Brunello. It has one of the longest minimum ageing periods of any Tuscan red. The Montalcino hill rises between the Orcia, Asso and Ombrone valleys.

Carmignano.atlas_note: Carmignano lies on the Montalbano ridge west of Florence, in the province of Prato. It was one of the four zones delimited by Cosimo III de' Medici in 1716. Its rules have long required Cabernet in the blend with Sangiovese.

Chianti.vine_area_src: ARTEA schedario viticolo, area registered as claimable (rivendicabile) for Chianti at 31 July 2024, 3,561 farms (Regione Toscana). The Consorzio Vino Chianti gives 15,500 ha (2024 brochure). ARTEA declarations for the 2014 harvest: 11,233 ha Chianti, 831.99 ha Chianti Superiore, 14,257.97 ha for Chianti with sottozone in all.
Chianti.atlas_note: Chianti is the largest DOCG of Tuscany. Its zone spreads over the provinces of Arezzo, Florence, Pisa, Pistoia, Prato and Siena and surrounds Chianti Classico. The amendment of 5 June 2026 lowered the Sangiovese minimum to 60%, added a Rose type and an eighth sottozona, Terre di Vinci. Chianti held about 41% of the claimed DOP area of the region in 2024.
rules: DOC by DPR 9 Aug 1967 (GU 217, 30 Aug 1967); DOCG by DPR 2 Jul 1984 (GU 290, 20 Oct 1984); last amendment DM 5 Jun 2026 (GU 134, 12 Jun 2026)
Chianti, Riserva and Rose, each with or without one of 8 sottozone; Superiore without sottozona (art. 1)
Sangiovese 60 to 100%; white grapes up to 10%; Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon up to 15%, 10% in Colli Senesi (art. 2)
Sangiovese at least 60%, rest from a listed set of white and black varieties (art. 2)
11 t/ha for Chianti and Rose; 9.5 t/ha for Superiore, Colli Aretini, Colline Pisane, Montalbano, Montespertoli, Rufina; 9 t/ha for Colli Fiorentini, Colli Senesi, Terre di Vinci (art. 4)
10.50% vol for Chianti and Rose; 11.50% vol for Superiore and all sottozone (art. 4)

1 March after harvest for Chianti, Colli Aretini, Colli Senesi, Colline Pisane, Montalbano; 1 June for Colli Fiorentini and Montespertoli; 1 September for Rufina, Superiore and Terre di Vinci; Rose from 1 December of the harvest year (art. 5)
At least 2 years from 1 January after harvest (art. 5)
11.50% vol Chianti and Rose; 12.00% vol with a sottozona; 12.50% vol Riserva and Superiore; 13.00% vol Colli Senesi Riserva (art. 6)
Governo all'uso toscano allowed; the term governato requires it (art. 5, art. 7)
Traditional Tuscan fiasco allowed but not for Rose; Riserva needs a flush cork; crown caps banned (art. 8)

Chianti Classico.atlas_note: Chianti Classico covers about 71,800 ha of hills between Florence and Siena. It lies wholly in four communes and partly in four more. It was a part of Chianti until 1996, when it became a DOCG with its own rules. Since 2023 its Gran Selezione wines may name one of 11 UGA.

7.5 t/ha and 2 kg per vine; vineyards up to 700 m (art. 4)

At least 24 months including 3 in bottle, from 1 January after harvest (art. 5)
At least 30 months including 3 in bottle; no enrichment (art. 5)

Bordeaux bottle or fiasco; fiasco banned for Riserva and Gran Selezione; flush cork (art. 8)

Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.vine_area_src: ARTEA schedario viticolo, registered as claimable (rivendicabile) for Vino Nobile at 31 July 2024: 1,389 ha, 258 farms (Regione Toscana). The Consorzio press kit 2024 gives about 1,300 ha on the DOCG albo, and 1,102 ha at 31 Dec 2023 (source ARTEA). The 1,102 ha is the area actually claimed for the 2023 harvest: the kit gives 7,797 t of grapes for it, 7.1 t/ha, just under the 8 t/ha limit. So 1,389 ha measures what may be claimed and 1,102 ha what was claimed in 2023.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.atlas_note: Vino Nobile comes from the commune of Montepulciano in the province of Siena, on a ridge between the Val di Chiana and the Val d'Orcia. Sangiovese is called Prugnolo Gentile here. Since 2025 the top non-Riserva wines may carry the mention Pieve with one of 12 UGA.
rules: DOC by DPR 12 Jul 1966; DOCG by DPR 1 Jul 1980 (GU 47, 17 Feb 1981); last amendment DM 21 Jan 2025 (GU 29, 5 Feb 2025)
Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) at least 70%; up to 30% other varieties, whites up to 5%; aromatic varieties banned except Malvasia Bianca Lunga (art. 2)
Sangiovese at least 85%; rest only Canaiolo Nero, Ciliegiolo, Mammolo and Colorino (Colorino up to 5%) (art. 2)
250 to 600 m; at least 3,330 vines/ha; Pieve vines at least 15 years old (art. 4)
8 t/ha; Pieve 7 t/ha and 2.5 kg per vine (art. 4)
2 years from 1 January after harvest, at least 1 year in wood: 24 months in wood, or 18 in wood, or 12 in wood plus 6 in bottle (art. 5)
At least 3 years including 6 months in bottle (art. 5)
Only for non-Riserva wine; at least 3 years from 1 January after harvest including 12 months in wood and 12 in bottle; estate grapes; name of one of 12 UGA (art. 1, art. 5, Annex A)
Dark Bordeaux bottle up to 5 l, flush cork (art. 8)

Bolgheri.atlas_note: Bolgheri lies on the coastal plain and foothills of the commune of Castagneto Carducci, in the province of Livorno, east of the old Via Aurelia. It was recognised by DPR of 1 August 1983, and the decree of 5 November 1994 added the Sassicaia sub-zone. Its reds are based on Bordeaux varieties, which sets it apart from the Sangiovese zones of inland Tuscany.

Whites 12 t/ha; Rosato and Rosso 9 t/ha; Superiore 8 t/ha (art. 4)
Rosso from 1 September of the year after harvest (art. 5)
At least 2 years from 1 January after harvest, at least 1 year in oak (art. 5)
Rosso and Superiore in dark Bordeaux bottles; Superiore with flush cork (art. 8)

Terre di Vinci.boundary_note: New in DM 5 Jun 2026. The line starts at Bivio Tesi in Lamporecchio, follows the Firenze-Pistoia border to Casa Barzi, runs through Vinci, Sant'Ansano, Collegonzi and Limite to the Arno at Sovigliana, then west by SP 11 and SS 446 through Cerreto Guidi and Fucecchio and back by Cerbaia and Varignano. It names the borders Lamporecchio-Cerreto Guidi, Vinci-Capraia e Limite, Vinci-Cerreto Guidi, Cerreto Guidi-Fucecchio and Lamporecchio-Larciano. Its area overlaps the Montalbano line in Vinci, Lamporecchio, Larciano and Capraia e Limite; how the overlap is handled is not stated.
